title: How to Think
author: Holly Korbey
summary: Korbey discusses the importance of effortful thinking in student learning, focusing on research from Meg Lee and Jim Heal of Learning Science Partners. While knowledge-building has gained prominence in education, the article emphasizes that what students do with knowledge determines learning outcomes. The research identifies four big ideas about effortful thinking that teachers and leaders should understand: thinking is cognitively demanding and requires deliberate support, students must actively work with knowledge to learn it deeply, schools must create environments that promote effortful thinking, and recognizing quality student thinking requires specific pedagogical awareness. The article argues that schools often underestimate the cognitive effort required for genuine learning and fail to structure instruction to make thinking visible and productive. Korbey concludes that leading students to knowledge is insufficient—the real challenge lies in creating conditions where students engage in the hard cognitive work of making meaning from that knowledge.
points: Effortful thinking is cognitively demanding, and schools must deliberately structure environments to make thinking more likely.
Knowledge acquisition is insufficient for learning: students must work with knowledge, connecting new ideas to existing understanding.
Teachers and leaders need specific skills to recognize and support quality student thinking.
Students have natural resistance to effortful thinking, yet sustained cognitive effort is non-negotiable for deep learning.
Schools must intentionally design for effortful thinking rather than defaulting to passive knowledge consumption.
